name: Nathu La
tagline: The 4,310 m border pass on the old Lhasa road, for Indians only
meta_description: Nathu La from Gangtok: who may visit, permit rules, open days, car costs, the 1958 road, 1967 clashes, 2006 trade reopening and altitude safety.
summary: Nathu La is a pass at 4,310 m on the India–China border, about 54 km and 2.5–3 hours from Gangtok. Only Indian citizens may visit, with a permit arranged a day ahead by a registered operator, on set days of the week. A reserved car with Tsomgo and Baba Mandir costs about ₹5,500–7,500.

local_story.title: The listening-ears pass on the road to Lhasa
paras: Nathu La is usually explained as the listening-ears pass, sometimes as the whistling pass, la being Tibetan for pass. It crosses the Dongkya Range between Sikkim and the Chumbi valley of Tibet. J. W. Edgar surveyed it in 1873 and found Tibetans trading over it. Francis Younghusband's expedition used it in 1903–04, and for the first half of the 20th century mule trains carried wool, salt and tea over Nathu La and its neighbour Jelep La, about 4.8 km away, between Lhasa, Gangtok and Kalimpong.

Work to make the Gangtok–Nathu La road fit for motor vehicles began in 1954. Jawaharlal Nehru formally opened it on 17 September 1958, in the presence of the Chogyal of Sikkim; the motor road then ended at Sherathang, below the pass. Two years earlier, in 1956, the Dalai Lama had crossed Nathu La to India for the 2,500th Buddha Jayanti. After the 1962 war the pass was sealed, and in September 1967 Indian and Chinese troops fought here, with deaths on both sides.

Ties slowly improved. Indian tourists were allowed up to the pass from 1999, and on 6 July 2006 Nathu La reopened for border trade, with a trade mart at Sherathang. From 2015 it became a second route for Indian pilgrims to Kailash and Mansarovar. Today soldiers of the two armies stand only metres apart across a fence, and the pass is one of the five points where they hold formal Border Personnel Meetings.

did_you_know: Twice a week, on Thursdays and Sundays, Indian and Chinese postmen exchange international surface mail at Nathu La's Sherathang post, a handover lasting only a few minutes.
The Gangtok–Nathu La road was formally opened by Jawaharlal Nehru on 17 September 1958, when the motor road ended at Sherathang below the pass.
Nathu La reopened for India–China border trade on 6 July 2006, after decades sealed; trade runs only on set weekdays and for about seven to eight months a year.
intro: Nathu La is the end of the road for tourists in East Sikkim, and the highest point most visitors to Gangtok reach. The drive from town climbs from 1,650 m to 4,310 m in about 54 km, past Tsomgo Lake and the new Baba Mandir, into bare, windswept country of rock, snow and army camps. At the top, a short climb of steps from the parking area leads to a viewing area near the fence, with Chinese soldiers and buildings visible just across it.

It is a place to visit for its history and its height rather than for comfort. The air is thin, the wind fierce and the weather changes fast. Only Indian citizens may go, on a permit arranged a day ahead in Gangtok, and the pass opens to tourists only on certain days of the week, usually not Mondays or Tuesdays. Snow, army orders and border tensions can close it at short notice. Check current status before you travel.
facts: India–China border, Silk Route history, snow
costs: Reserved car, Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La

highlights.title: The border fence
highlights.text: From the parking area, steps climb to a viewing area by the fence at 4,310 m, with Chinese soldiers and buildings only metres away. Indian soldiers explain the rules on the spot. Photography is limited, so follow their instructions exactly and do not wave, shout or point cameras where told not to.

highlights.title: The road above Tsomgo
highlights.text: Beyond Tsomgo Lake the road leaves the last trees and climbs through open slopes of rock, scree and snow. On clear days you see ridge after bare ridge, small lakes in hollows and army camps along the way. It is one of the highest motor roads most Indian tourists will ever travel.

highlights.title: The new Baba Mandir
highlights.text: On the way back most cars stop at the shrine to Sepoy Harbhajan Singh, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968. Army tradition holds that his spirit still guards the border. Soldiers keep the shrine, and visitors leave bottles of water to be blessed.

highlights.title: The old trade road
highlights.text: Nathu La and Jelep La, about 4.8 km apart, carried the wool, salt and tea trade between Lhasa and Kalimpong until 1962. Since 6 July 2006, licensed traders have again crossed at Nathu La on set days. The trade mart at Sherathang lies below the pass.

highlights.title: Snow in summer
highlights.text: At 4,310 m snow can lie around the pass well into May and fresh falls are possible in any month outside the monsoon. For families from the plains, Nathu La in April or May is often the first chance to see deep snow without the January cold.

highlights.title: A history lesson at the top
highlights.text: The pass saw Younghusband's column in 1903–04, the Dalai Lama's crossing in 1956, Nehru's road in 1958 and the clashes of September 1967. Army boards near the pass tell some of the story. Ask the soldiers questions politely; many are glad to talk.

how_to_reach.text: Almost everyone goes in a reserved Sikkim-registered car booked through a registered Gangtok operator, usually combined with Tsomgo and Baba Mandir, for about ₹5,500–7,500. The operator applies for the permit a day ahead with your photo ID and passport photos.

Some Gangtok tour desks sell shared seats to Nathu La on its open days, for roughly ₹1,500–2,500 including the permit. Availability depends on demand and permit quotas, so ask a day or two ahead. It is the cheapest way for solo travellers and pairs.

Private and outside vehicles are generally not allowed beyond the checkposts, and permits are tied to registered tourist vehicles. Leave your own car in Gangtok. Rules change, so check current status before you travel.

where_to_stay: There is nowhere for tourists to stay at Nathu La; it is a military area and a day trip, and cars must return in the afternoon. Sleep in Gangtok, 2.5–3 hours below, where you can find dorm beds and plain rooms near MG Marg, family-run guesthouses such as Mintokling and Netuk House, and budget hotels on the lower roads. A good night's sleep in Gangtok before the trip helps with the altitude. If you want to stay higher, the Silk Route homestays at Gnathang and Zuluk are reached by a different permit.
tips: Spend at least one night in Gangtok before going to Nathu La, and do not attempt it on the day you arrive from the plains.
Carry an original photo ID on the day, as well as the copies you gave for the permit; soldiers check at several posts.
Climb the steps to the viewing area very slowly and stay no more than 20–30 minutes at the top.
Follow every instruction from soldiers about photography and where to stand; this is an active border.
Start early, because weather at the pass often turns in the afternoon and vehicles must head down by a set time.

experiences.title: At the fence on the India–China border
experiences.best_time: Late morning on open days, Apr–Jun and Oct–Nov
experiences.cost: Included in your car and permit
experiences.summary: A short, slow climb of steps from the parking area at Nathu La leads to a viewing area beside the border fence at 4,310 m. Chinese soldiers and buildings stand only metres away. It is cold, windy and short, and you follow the soldiers' rules.
body: Cars stop at a parking area just below the pass, and from there a flight of steps climbs to the viewing area. At 4,310 m those steps are harder than they look: climb slowly, stop often and do not race children to the top. At the fence, barbed wire and a low barrier mark the border, with Chinese soldiers and their buildings only metres away. There is no no-man's-land here, which is what makes the place so striking.

Indian soldiers manage the visitors and explain what you may and may not do. Photography is restricted, and the rules change with the situation, so ask before raising a camera and put it away if told. Shouting, waving at the other side, flying drones and crossing any marked line are forbidden. In the past tourists shook hands across the fence; do not expect it now.

Twenty to thirty minutes at the top is plenty. The wind cuts through most jackets, and the thin air makes some people dizzy or breathless. If anyone feels unwell, go down to the car at once. On the way back, look out across the bare ridges towards Jelep La and Kupup, and stop at Baba Mandir and Tsomgo Lake as you descend.

faqs.q: Can we take photos at Nathu La?
faqs.a: Only where and when the soldiers allow. Photography rules at Nathu La are set by the army and change with the situation; some days you may photograph the fence area, other days not. Ask first, never photograph military installations or personnel without permission, and put your camera away if told. Drones are banned.

faqs.q: Can we see Chinese soldiers at Nathu La?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Chinese soldiers and buildings stand only metres away across the fence. Do not wave, shout, signal or try to talk across the border. In earlier years visitors shook hands across the fence, but rules have tightened since 2020. Follow the Indian soldiers' instructions at all times.

faqs.q: How long can we stay at Nathu La?
faqs.a: Most visitors spend about 20–30 minutes at the viewing area. Vehicles must head down by a set time, usually early afternoon, and longer stays at 4,310 m raise the risk of altitude sickness. Climb the steps slowly and go down at once if anyone feels dizzy or sick.

experiences.title: The shrine of Baba Harbhajan Singh
experiences.best_time: On the way down from Nathu La, all year
experiences.summary: A shrine kept by the Indian Army to Sepoy Harbhajan Singh of the Punjab Regiment, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968. Soldiers believe his spirit still guards the border. It is the most visited stop on the Nathu La road after Tsomgo.
body: Harbhajan Singh was born in 1946 and joined the Indian Army in 1965. He died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968. Army tradition holds that his spirit continued to serve: soldiers tell of him appearing in dreams to warn of danger, and the shrine built in his memory became a place of faith for the troops posted on this border. Whatever you believe, it is treated with complete seriousness here, and visitors should do the same.

There are two shrines. The original, often called the old Baba Mandir, is a bunker shrine on the far side of the ridge towards Kupup and Gnathang, reached on the Silk Route. The one most Nathu La visitors see is the newer, larger shrine on the main road between Tsomgo and the pass, built by the army in 1982 to be easier to reach. Inside are his photograph, his uniform and boots, and a room kept as if he still lived there.

Visitors leave bottles of water to be blessed and collect them on the way out; many believe the water helps the sick. Remove shoes before entering, cover your head if asked and keep your voice down. Soldiers on duty may tell the story; listen and thank them. There is usually a small army-run shop or canteen nearby for tea.

faqs.q: Who was Baba Harbhajan Singh?
faqs.a: Harbhajan Singh was a soldier of the Punjab Regiment, born in 1946, who died near Nathu La on 4 October 1968. Army tradition holds that his spirit still guards the border and warns soldiers of danger. The shrine to him on the Nathu La road is kept by the army and visited by thousands.

faqs.q: What is the difference between old and new Baba Mandir?
faqs.a: The old Baba Mandir is the original bunker shrine on the Silk Route side of the ridge, near Kupup and Gnathang. The new Baba Mandir, built by the army in 1982, stands on the main road between Tsomgo and Nathu La and is the one most day trips visit. Both are respected equally.

faqs.q: Is Baba Mandir included in a Tsomgo trip?
faqs.a: Usually yes. Shared Tsomgo tours and reserved cars normally include the new Baba Mandir, about 30–45 minutes beyond the lake, even if you do not go on to Nathu La. Confirm with your operator when you book, as permits and road conditions sometimes stop trips at Tsomgo.

experiences.title: The trade road and the 1967 clashes
experiences.best_time: Any open day, Apr–Jun and Oct–Nov
experiences.wiki: Nathu La and Cho La clashes
experiences.summary: Nathu La's story runs from mule trains carrying wool to Kalimpong, through Nehru's motor road of 1958 and the clashes of September 1967, to the trade mart at Sherathang that reopened in 2006. Knowing it turns a cold half hour at the fence into something more.
body: For centuries Nathu La and nearby Jelep La were the main gates between Tibet and the hills of Sikkim and Bengal. Wool, musk and yak tails came south; cloth, tools, tea and sugar went north. After Britain's 1903–04 expedition to Lhasa used the pass, trade grew steadily, and in the 1950s much of Sikkim's trade still crossed here. The motor road from Gangtok, opened by Nehru on 17 September 1958, ended at Sherathang, below the pass; beyond it, goods still went on mules.

The 1962 war closed the border. In September 1967, a dispute over fencing at the pass turned into fighting between Indian and Chinese troops, followed by a clash at Cho La in October; both sides lost men. The border here stayed tense but quiet for decades afterwards. Domestic tourists were first allowed up in 1999, and on 6 July 2006 Nathu La reopened for trade, with traders crossing on set weekdays to a mart at Sherathang.

You will see some of this from the road: the Sherathang trade buildings, army camps and memorial boards. Ask your driver to point them out. Trade volumes have stayed modest, limited by snow to seven or eight months a year and by a short list of goods. Border tensions and the pandemic halted trade and pilgrimages from 2020; whether they have resumed is worth asking in Gangtok.

faqs.q: What happened at Nathu La in 1967?
faqs.a: In September 1967 a dispute over the border fence at Nathu La turned into fighting between Indian and Chinese troops, followed in October by a clash at nearby Cho La. Both sides suffered deaths. The fighting ended within days, and the border here has since been held by both armies at very close quarters.

faqs.q: Is trade still happening at Nathu La?
faqs.a: Border trade reopened through Nathu La on 6 July 2006, on set weekdays, with a trade mart at Sherathang. It was halted from 2020 by border tensions and the pandemic. Whether it is running when you visit depends on current agreements, so ask in Gangtok and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Can tourists visit the Sherathang trade mart?
faqs.a: Tourists usually see the Sherathang trade mart only from the road on the way to Nathu La. It is meant for licensed traders, not shoppers, and access is controlled. Ask your driver to point it out, but do not expect to stop and shop there.

experiences.title: A full day to Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La
experiences.best_time: Leave 7 am on open days, Apr–Jun and Oct–Nov
experiences.summary: The classic East Sikkim day: up past Tsomgo Lake to Nathu La at 4,310 m, back via the new Baba Mandir and a lakeside lunch. It is long, high and cold, and needs a permit arranged a day ahead. Split a reserved car between four or five to keep it cheap.
body: Book the day through a registered Gangtok operator at least a day ahead, handing over photo ID copies and passport photos for each person. Indian citizens only: if anyone in your group is a foreign national, plan Tsomgo instead. The car leaves Gangtok around 7 am, passes the Kyongnosla checkpost and climbs through the rhododendron forest to Tsomgo Lake. Most drivers go straight on to Nathu La first, to reach the pass before the afternoon weather.

Above Tsomgo the trees end and the road climbs through bare high country to the parking area below the pass. Spend 20–30 minutes at the viewing area, then descend to the new Baba Mandir for half an hour. Come back down to Tsomgo for a late lunch of thukpa or noodles at the stalls and a short walk along the shore, and reach Gangtok by about 4–5 pm.

Dress in layers, with a down jacket, gloves and a hat from October to May, and hire boots on the way in snowy months. Drink water through the day, eat light and avoid alcohol the night before. Do not do this trip on your first day in the hills. If snow closes the road beyond Tsomgo, operators usually offer Tsomgo and Baba Mandir only; ask how the price changes before you pay. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How much does a Nathu La trip cost from Gangtok?
faqs.a: A reserved car covering Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La costs about ₹5,500–7,500 in 2025–26, including permits arranged by the operator. Shared seats, when offered, cost about ₹1,500–2,500. Boot hire, food and the Tsomgo ropeway are extra. Prices rise in October and May.

faqs.q: What documents do we need for the Nathu La permit?
faqs.a: Indian citizens usually need a copy of a photo ID such as an Aadhaar card, voter ID or passport, plus two passport photos per person, given to a registered operator a day ahead. Carry the originals on the day. Children's ID rules vary, so ask the operator. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: What if Nathu La is closed on our day?
faqs.a: If snow, weather or army orders close Nathu La, operators usually run Tsomgo and Baba Mandir instead, with a lower price. Agree the refund or price difference before you book. Keep a spare day in Gangtok so you can try again on the next open day.

faqs.q: Who can visit Nathu La?
faqs.a: Only Indian citizens may visit Nathu La, with a permit arranged a day ahead through a registered Gangtok operator, using a photo ID and passport photos. Foreign nationals, including OCI holders, are not allowed and usually visit Tsomgo Lake instead. Rules can change, so check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Which days is Nathu La open for tourists?
faqs.a: Nathu La usually opens to tourists on four or five days a week and stays shut on Mondays and Tuesdays, but the days change with army orders, snow and border conditions, and closures can come at short notice. Ask your operator when you apply for the permit, and check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: How far is Nathu La from Gangtok?
faqs.a: About 54 km, which takes 2.5–3 hours each way on a steep mountain road past Tsomgo Lake. A full day covering Tsomgo, Baba Mandir and Nathu La takes about 8–9 hours, leaving Gangtok around 7 am. Vehicles must head down from the pass by early afternoon.

faqs.q: How high is Nathu La?
faqs.a: Nathu La is at 4,310 m (14,140 ft), more than 2,600 m above Gangtok. Most people feel the height: breathlessness, headaches and tiredness are common. Spend a night in Gangtok first, climb the steps slowly, drink water and go down at once if anyone feels very unwell.

faqs.q: Is Nathu La safe for children and senior citizens?
faqs.a: Healthy older children and fit seniors usually manage a short visit, but the altitude is serious. Infants, pregnant women and people with heart, lung or blood-pressure problems should take medical advice and may be better off stopping at Tsomgo. Keep everyone warm, move slowly and stay only 20–30 minutes.

faqs.q: What is the best time to visit Nathu La?
faqs.a: April to June and October to November give the best mix of open roads and clear skies. From December to March snow often closes the pass for days, though it can be open between falls. From July to September landslides and cloud make the trip uncertain. Check current status before you travel.

faqs.q: Does it snow at Nathu La?
faqs.a: Yes. Snow usually covers Nathu La from about December to April and can fall in any month outside the monsoon. Even in May, patches of deep snow are common around the pass. Heavy falls close the road until it is cleared. Wear boots with grip and dress for well below freezing.

faqs.q: Can we go to Nathu La by our own car?
faqs.a: Generally no. Permits are issued with Sikkim-registered tourist vehicles booked through registered operators, and private or outside vehicles are stopped at the checkposts. Hire a local car or join a shared seat in Gangtok. Check current status before you travel, as rules occasionally change.

faqs.q: Is there mobile network at Nathu La?
faqs.a: Usually weak or none, and in places phones may pick up foreign networks near the border, which can bring roaming charges. Set your phone to avoid roaming or switch to flight mode near the pass. Tell family you will be offline for most of the day.
